(i) we observe an even-odd oscillations in the second harmonic generation efficiency of WS2 and (WSe2) multilayer samples which is a direct signature of inversion symmetry breaking, and (ii) we observe a hot luminescence band in the photoluminescence spectra of WS2 and and WSe2 samples which we attribute to spin-valley coupling.

the optical signature of symmetry variations, spin-valley coupling and the band structure evolution in atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides, which provides a fundamental understanding of these materials and may open new opportunities in optoelectronic applications.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the optical properties of WS2 and/or WSe2 monofolayers and multifolayers can be well understood by the symmetry variations and spin-orbit coupling.

, (1) WS2/WSe2 monolayer is a direct band gap semiconductor with giant spin-valley splitting, (2) the band structure of multilayers is a superposition of monolayer and bulk bands with a crossover from indirect to direct gap, and (3) the spin-valley interaction is robust in multilayers and is responsible for the even-odd thickness oscillation of second harmonic generation and the thickness independent A-B splitting in photoluminescence.

the optical signature of symmetry variations in atomically thin transition metal dichalcogenides is revealed, which can be a useful guide in the design and fabrication of novel optoelectronic and valleytronics devices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spin-valley physics in monolayer TMDs can be extended to multilayer systems, and the spin-valley splitting can be used to distinguish between even-layer and odd-layer structures.
the spin-valley splitting in WS2/WSe2 is a robust phenomenon that can be directly probed by optical measurements.
the thickness-dependent symmetry variations and the giant spin-valency coupling in tungsten dichalcgenides are revealed by optical studies.
